That's a good point.

Anyway, I'm not familiar enough with this argument anymore to properly explain or defend it, so I'm gonna drop it. It's not really my cup of tea anyway. I'm gonna move onto another issue that I'm more interested in and understand much better.

But before I start, I've got a question. You all do believe you've got free will, right? I'm gonna assume you all do. The question then, is, if an omniscient God has existed all along, how on earth does that change anything? You still would have made all the same choices, and you would still go on to make all the same choices you will. This a crucially important point.

You make the choices. You are the one determining your future. God only knows what you will do tomorrow because its what you will do. Its sounds stupid and tautological, but really its that simple. You would have done the same thing had there not been any God in the first place.

The definition Iangb gave for free will makes it so that free will is impossible under any reasonable scenario. Requiring this metaphysical ability to have made choices other than the ones you in fact did makes it so that there is no possible world in which free will can exist. Free will cannot be about being able to choose other than you in fact did because you can never make any choices other than the one you did. You made the choice, and you only get to do it once. Those two facts alone make it impossible to choose other than you in fact did.

But were talking about the future, not the past. There should be real possibilities for choices we havent made yet, right? Tomorrow, I might have coffee or I might have orange juice. If God already knows which one you will choose, so, in effect, theres only one real choice. Its a very forceful argument when its put this way, and it feels like your choice is constrained by gods knowledge. But this is a distraction. Its a red herring. This argument is phrased in such a way that it makes people miss whats really going on.

The real point is that theres only one real choice because you only get to make one choice. The original argument gets its force solely from this point, but it twists it and abuses a definition of free will that seems intuitive but is actually misleading, in order to force the conclusion that free will cannot exist alongside an omniscient god.

You probably think Im missing the point, but trust me, Im not. You think that for free will to exist, at this time there have to be multiple possible paths for the future, and that gods knowledge makes it so that theres only one. I get it, trust me.

Now get what Im saying. Nothing is constraining your choices. You choose orange juice because you want to drink orange juice. Every single choice you make falls in line with your desires. Had you desired to do differently, then you would have done differently. This is all thats required for free will. And this definition conveniently makes free will compatible with both determinism and an omniscient god.

Quote: Daddaluma, 2006-03-30T00:24:50Z
You make the choices. You are the one determining your future. God only knows what you will do tomorrow because its what you will do. Its sounds stupid and tautological, but really its that simple. You would have done the same thing had there not been any God in the first place.

That's entirely the argument for predetermination. Which is exactly why I think that everything is indeed predetermined, because, simply, you will do what you will do. You're going to choose what you're going to choose, and that's that. It's not a matter so much of having the choice, but being as it is when you're presented with the choice, you can't choose both, because your mind is made up well before you even know what the choice is what you're going to do.

I don't like the term predetermined, because it makes it sound like something else is doing the deciding for you. I don't think this is the case. I think when you choose what to drink in the morning, you are the one making that choice right then, and it will be based on your desires at that time.

Yes, your desires are the inevitable end result of 13 billion years of history, but that doesn't change the fact that they are still your desires and you are free to act according to them. That's all free will is, the ability to act unconstrained according to our desires, or our "will" if you will.



Quote: Kablizzy, 2006-03-30T00:48:14Z
So, in that vein, it can easily be said that, taking desires into account, that Free Will is an illusion. When you choose what you choose, you choose that option for a reason beyond your own understanding, and that option which you choose couldn't have been chosen any differently.

It's not as though you're really, actually *choosing* anything, right?  I mean, you know, on a level that you can't consciously understand, whether you'll drink coffee or orange juice tomorrow morning. Why? Because the events during the night will determine the type of rest you will get. Conditions around you will lead you to either getting a good night's sleep, or a bad night's sleep. Taking this simple hypothetical a step farther, let's say, arbitrarily that, if you get a bad night's sleep, that you'll drink coffee, since it will be harder for you to awaken tomorrow morning, and you'll feel as though you need the boost for the day. If you get a good night's sleep, you'll drink orange juice.

So, now, let's take it one step farther, to where you are. Let's say you get a horrible night's sleep, but decide to drink orange juice anyway, because you're choosing, for whatever reason, to ignore how tired you are, and drink orange juice. It's that very reason that you decide whether to ignore events or not which is in contention. But I'm putting forth that the reason that you either decide to go with the status quo or not go with the status quo is solely and entirely dependant upon predetermined factors that we, as humans, can neither comprehend, nor see.

I dont see how any of this changes the fundamental point that all of our actions are the direct result of what we consciously desire. A tree doesnt have the power to act according to its desires, but we do, and yet both our actions and the trees actions are equally determined. We can all see the difference between us and a tree, and this difference is the only thing thats important for free will. Free will is not an illusion. The only illusion is that free will requires that we somehow be separate from the physical universe and not subject to its laws.


Quote: Kablizzy, 2006-03-30T00:48:14Z
Following from that, each and every one of those factors, no matter how large, small, or insignificant, influences each of our decisions to the point where we feel as though the insignificant ones *are* indeed insignificant. But they aren't. And here's why;

We tend to ignore the things upon which we deem insignificant. But if we were to take every last deciding factor into account for any given decision, and if we were able to analyze, and say, assign a point value, positive or negative, to every event or thought or reaction, or conditional in your life, as it pertains to any given event, choice, or decision, we could easily track what a person's given decision would be, based upon said numbers, positive being one choice, and negative being another. The fact that we can't, and probably never will, be able to track or determine a good majority of those factors, or assign any type of numerical significance values to it, doesn't lend anything to the credibility or discredit of the thought.

Am I making sense on that?

Of course youre making sense. Youre simply describing exactly what determinism is. Most people have this conception that determinism means that the future is predetermined (which seems to imply that some other intelligence has already decided what the future should be). Thats not really what it means. Determinism simply is the thought that theres nothing outside of the physical laws of nature and that those govern everything 100 percent so that each given instant is the 100% inevitable result of those laws and the past.

However, as I argued above, this doesnt make a lick of difference as to whether or not we have free will.

In which case, it seems, the point of contention comes into play as to whether we have desires and a soul, and a seperate conscience away from the laws of the physical realm, or whether all of that is simply a mass of chemical reactions to create such things as sentience, and awareness, and higher thought. And, on this, I'm not sure. I couldn't claim one way or the other on it. Your tree analogy is intriguing, but is there any way that we can know that solely because we have a brainstem and certain chemical reactions in our head that a tree does not, that is what causes/allows our level of awareness?
I like to leave out discussion of a soul since it's pure nonsense and anything said about it is nothing more than speculation based on . . . well based on nothing really. Any discussion about the soul is nothing more than science fiction.

However, for the crazies among us who like to think that they have an immortal aphysical soul which somehow allows them to circumvent the laws of nature, I'll give it a shot.

Let's just assume that the soul is an immortal spirit which has absolutely no physical properties. Obviously, it's unclear how such a soul could ever interact with the physical world, but whatever, let's let that slide. So we've got a soul, and the soul is free, not determined. Theoretically, this soul would allow the following scenario:

Quote: Fantasy Time
At time T, I am deciding between coffee and orange juice.  I happen to select orange juice.  But since I have a soul, if time were somehow reversed, and it became time T again, well this time I just might choose to drink coffee.

Remove the bit about having a soul, and this is exactly what many people misconceive free will to mean. Adding in the soul supposedly adds in a way for us to get around the fact that purely physical being are nothing more than the result of natural laws, and as such, at time T a purely physical being would choose orange juice every single time.

However, this doesn't seem to me to be any more free than a deterministic universe. All that's happening is the soul is magically changing our desires from orange juice to coffee. If this change has a cause, then it can be predicted and we're back to where we started: a determined future. If this change does not have a cause, then it's random, and I don't see how that makes us any more free than as we currently are. Under both scenarios (fantasy and determined universe), we still have the ability to perform actions according to our desires. The only difference is that in one of the two scenarios, our desires are random, fanciful and not subject to reason or laws.

Il comando di vertice dell'Esercito Italiano rappresentato dallo "Stato Maggiore dellEsercito" a Roma, il quale ha il compito di fissare le linee "politiche" relative all'addestramento, all'equipaggiamento e all'impiego del personale, nonch elaborare la dottrina e formulare i progetti di evoluzione futura dello strumento militare terrestre nazionale. Per l'attivit di comando e controllo sulle unit dell'Esercito, Il Capo di Stato Maggiore dell'Esercito (che dipende a sua volta dal Capo di Stato Maggiore della Difesa) si avvale di una serie di Comandi e Ispettorati retti da Ufficiali Generali. I don't see how the PS3 can possibly said to be winning. The page they stole out of nintendo's book, you know, the motion sensing controller (without the need for a sensor!)? Not to mention that the Wii was designed from the ground up to support the motion sensing functions, whereas Sony just threw that together in the last year. How many games do you think are going to make use of those motion sensing functions in any sort of creative way? Certainly none of the launch titles.

Oh, and speaking of launch titles, how many playable demos does Sony have at E3? I don't actually know the answer, but I doubt they've got many. What's more they probably aren't even running the demos on real PS3 hardware.

Whereas nintendo has 27 different games available to try out, all of which are actually running on the Wii hardware.

I watched Nintendo's presentation yesterday, and while I knew exactly what to expect out of the control and gameplay, I was still stunned and elated watching 4 people actually play a stupid tennis game on the wii. The game itself couldn't have been simpler, too, and yet it still looked more fun than just about anything I've seen coming out of E3 yet.

I'm firmly in Nintendo's camp this time around. And I'm betting that they ome out with the number 1 console in this generation.

Hailing from the Wild and Wooly Uncharted West, Gar is as rugged and uncouth as they come. Raised by a pack of coyotes, he never quite learned any social skills, manners, or personal hygiene. 1. Clearly nintendo wins in terms of pure price. However, it's my guess (but an educated one) that Nintendo will make some profit off each console sale. Meaning that the Wii hardware costs less than 200 dollars to manufacture. Whereas the PS3 is going to be losing about 300 dollars on every single console they sell even at 600 dollars.

So in terms of pure economic value, the PS3 wins.

2. Umm?

3. Nintendo wins this one, no contest. PS3 is not offering anything original at all.

4. The controller. Obviously Wii's biggest point. Sony doesn't offer anything terribly interesting in the controller department. Their motion sensing controller strikes me as pointless. It might come into effect in a few games, but it fees more like an afterthought than anything. I'm not even sure why they bothered.

5. Nintendo makes nearly it's entire back catalog of games available to Wii owners. However, Sony makes it's entire back catalog available too. Nintendo has a longer history and nostalgia on its side, so it wins this round too.

Well that does it for your list. You've got Nintendo's main selling points on there. However, you ask, what does Sony have against what Nintendo is offering? Let me offer you a list of my own.

1. HD gaming. If you've got the money, the HD experience is something truly marvelous to behold. In terms of graphic upgrades, this is a biggy. Nintendo is not supporting any HD at all.

2. Vastly more powerful hardware. Yes I'm sure Nintendo is going to squeeze out every last bit of graphic prowess they can from their machine, and the games will probably look really nice. But unlike the power gap between gamecube and xbox, this time it will be immediately obvious. Sure, graphics don't make a game fun, but they do turn a fun game into one hell of a visual experience. Plus there are games which absolutely depend on the graphics. Shadow of the Colossus? The game is widely lauded for it's innovative gaming experience, but the game would be absolute crap with bad graphics. Contrary to what many "enlightened" people like to say, graphics can be crucially important to a game. Also, more power and more space on the media opens up alot of doors to developers for Sony that aren't open to the Wii. Just like the Wii's controller opens up lots of avenues not possible for Sony.

3. A Blu-ray drive. If Blu-ray wins the format war, then the PS3 would be a very cheap blu-ray player. It would be a decent if you bought it solely for the blu-ray drive itself. I imagine many people are thinking, "I don't have an HDTV, this is all meaningless to me." Well I'm betting that a large portion of those thinking that aren't thinking very far ahead. In 3 years or so when all TV will be broadcast in HD broadcasts, and pretty much the only new tv's you can buy are HDTVs, it's more likely than not that you or your family will cave in and buy one. And when you do, your PS3 will be ready to take full advantage of that. You're Wii, won't give you anything you didn't already have.

#9320 1 2006-06-08T06:10:44Z Daddaluma
I'm tired of all these half assed games floating around, so I decided I would try to organize a game of Diplomacy for the forum.

You'll want to read the complete rules if you're going to play, but they're long, so I'll give you a quick synopsis of everything first so you can decide if this sounds interesting before you devote a couple of hours to reading the rules.

1. This game is like risk, except nothing is based on chance.
2. The object is to take over every country on the map.
3. The entire game revolves around negotiating with other players. You will be given considerable time to discuss strategy and make deals with the other players. However, no deal is binding, and up until each player's orders are submitted, nothing is final.

4. Once the orders for a turn are all in, all moves are resolved simultaneously. The game board will be updated and then the next round of negotiation can begin.

If you're interested sign up here and begin to read the full rules so everything makes more sense. After you've read the rules, feel free to ask any questions you have.

The full rules can be found here: Warning! Annoying PDF file ahoy

Edit: Also, if anyone's good with photoshop let me know. I suck at using it, and I'd like to pawn off the image editing duties on someone else.

Edit 2: Removed the picture. Check the wikipedia page is you want to see the board: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomacy_(game)

#239928 12 2006-10-12T04:23:58Z Daddaluma
I've thought about this kind of issue before too. It's one of the problems with libertarianism. There are a myriad of other similar examples you can raise as well. Most of them involve drawing a line in the gray somewhere.

In this case the stinker could reasonably be said to be infringing on everyone's right not to be forced to smell the stink. Although, then it could equally be said that the people aren't actually being forced to at all. They can freely leave and choose not be around the guy. Neither of them has a "right" to eat at the restaurant, so, it's not a problem with a clear cut right answer.

Do the people have the right to ban this guy from restaurants? I'd say no. If the restaurant owner for some odd reason chooses to do nothing about the guy, then that's the end of it, and the public either deals with it, or chooses not to eat there anymore.

#240363 49 2006-10-13T01:59:43Z Daddaluma
I feel the need to remind those of you that are arguing on the side of protecting the people's right to not have to smell offensive odors, that we are not talking about public property. If we were, I'd side with you guys.

But we're talking about private property here. Is it ok for the government to tell someone they can't stink when they're on their own property? Clearly not. Why, then, should it be ok for the government to tell me, I can't stink when I'm a guest on your private property?

My answer is simple. It's not. If you, the owner of the property, want to allow me to be there, foul-ass smell and all, then you should have every right to do that.

#240836 62 2006-10-14T02:14:51Z Daddaluma
The most important distinction I see is that in one case we're talking about an employer creating unsafe/unfair working conditions for his employees. And on the other side, we've got a business owner creating supposedly unsafe conditions for his patrons.

Employees often don't have a great degree of choice in where they work. I see alot of people taking whatever jobs they can get. So that means employers would have a lot more leeway to take advantage of their employees if they weren't regulated, simply because they've got a captive audience.

Patrons, unlike, employees, usually have tremendous fexibility in choosing where they take their business. Even if there was only one restaurant in town, the people still can easily decide to not go there without suffering any significant degree of harm to their lifestyle.

So, that's one way to draw a line.

A few issues here. The first three provisions of the amendment would get rid of welfare, social security and health care, and much of the rest of the list as it would go on eliminating the need to pay for them. It doesnt eliminate the possibility for states to recreate smaller versions of these programs. It simply stops the central federal government from becoming unbelievably big and powerful which was the original intent of the constitution.

Federal funding for education is completely unnecessary, and furthermore doesnt come from the income tax anyway. Your local property taxes pay for the vast majority of education spending. On a sidenote, is there anyone here who thinks the no child left behind act was a good thing? Ask pretty much any teacher you know in a public school and theyll tell you just how destructive to actual education it is. Federal control of education is a terrible idea. State control of education is still a bad thing, but much better than federal control at least.

The original constitution did not grant the federal government the power to tax peoples incomes. The framers of the constitution realized that the power to tax the incomes of the citizens would allow the government unchecked power. Our country survived fine for over 100 years without an income tax, and we only started one to pay for our expensive wars. Once the central government got the power to tax peoples incomes, though, they refused to give it up. The power to tax is the power to control, and governments are loathe to give up control.

#270480 8 2006-12-15T06:38:30Z Daddaluma
Here's my take.

All systems of morality must eventually boil down to some fundamental claim which is ultimately unprovable. So no system of morality can claim absolute truth.

However, this does not mean that there isn't one particular moral system which most or all could agree on which could be said to apply to all situations at all times. It just wouldn't be making "factual" claims.

If a certain fundamental axiom, or set of axioms could be agreed upon by everyone, then in effect, we have found our moral absolutes. Morality doesn't have to be a rigid set of one line, "thou shall not . . ." claims either. We can still claim moral absolutism, even with a system that allows for the same action in different situations to have different moral values.

#270515 42 2006-12-15T07:54:06Z Daddaluma
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarcho-capitalism

This wikipedia article should take care of all the basic problems you guys are having.

One thing to keep in mind is that while all these ideas probably strike you as crazy at first, when given just a bit of consideration, I think you'll find that they make perfect sense. That doesn't mean that you will like or agree with the outcome or the consequences, but as a system, it's perfectly viable.

For instance, to answer Kablizzy's question, what would happen to a guy who murdered someone? Private defense and courts can take care of this problem. There's nothing about the nature of policing or our court system that requires a government. Government backed courts don't have any more intrinsic legitimacy than private courts would.

But, to paint a more full scenario, private defense agencies would arise, sort of like insurance companies. Unlike the police, the goal of these companies would be to make money, so they're not going to want to go around shooting people or causing problems. And they wouldn't want their customers to go around shooting people or causing problems either.

Individuals would sign a contract with whatever company fit their needs best.

Let's say the guy who was murdered belonged to a Defense protection agency (DPA). That DPA would be responsible for tracking down and finding the killer. If the killer was a member of another DPA, then the two companies negotiate and agree on which private court they will use to settle the matter.

So, basically, exactly the same thing that happens now would happen under anarcho-capitalism, except everything is privately (and therefore more efficiently) run.
#270522 10 2006-12-15T08:23:28Z Daddaluma
Let me try to clarify just a bit.

If, for example, you made the claim that the bible is true, and therefore Morality is determined by god, you have made an unprovable claim. And since your entire morality system rests on an unprovable claim, it cannot be said to be fact.

This is true for every morality system you can think of though. For instance, if you said it's immoral to kill another person for no reason at all (something, I believe pretty much everyone would agree with), and I asked "why?" what would you say?

If you were a libertarian, you'd say that that person has a right not to have his body aggressed against and by killing him, you are violating his rights, which is wrong. But this claim, too, is an unprovable axiom. There's no inherent value in human life, and there's no rights which are intrinsic to the universe.

I suspect that was the part of what I said that wasn't all that confusing, so let me try to explain what the rest of what I said meant.

So, since all morality is based on a certain degree of subjectivity, it's value has to lie in how well it predicts our feelings toward events and actions. If everyone in the world agrees that it's immoral to torture a small child for fun, then any morality system which leads to any different conclusion has no value.

Now, we all know there are things which some people claim are immoral and others don't. Based solely on this fact, you might think that it's impossible for morality to be anything but relative. Take abortion for instance. McP thinks abortion is immoral, whereas, I do not. However, if we examine the underlying factors a bit, we might find that we are both working off the same fundamental moral claim. For instance, we both think it's wrong to murder innocent people, however, I don't think the fetus is a person. So it's not that we don't share the same morals, it's that we disagree on the facts of the situation.

So, what I'm saying now, and what I was trying to say before, is that even though on the surface we all make different moral evaluations and different situations result in different applications of our moral compass, we all might share the same fundamental axiom from which we derive our morality. And if this were the case, then we would have moral absolutism.

In terms of the overall American culture, that group that feels the need to devolve into a badass, or however you want to describe it, doesn't set the tone for all Americans. You and I don't feel pressure to "be true to our identity" by conforming to that group.

Whereas there's a great deal of pressure for an American black person to resist things that are considered "white". It takes tremendous strength of character for someone to rise above that pressure and actually go on to achieve.

Here's another great relevant article: http://www.eastbayexpress.com/2003-05-21/n...black-flunking/

You might want to read it before continuing.

This trend doesn't simply affect the impoverished, either. Black children from relatively wealthy families feel the same pressures to not act white. It also brings up some interesting ideas about voluntary immigrants versus involuntary immigrants. Native Americans and Black people born in this country still retain this idea that they're their own culture, and that anything they do that resembles conforming to society at large (such as speaking standard English and doing well in school) is a self betrayal.

Voluntary immigrants don't share these attitudes. They come here fully recognizing that they will have to learn the language to succeed, and that they'll have to work harder than the average person to overcome the resulting challenges. They also recognize that learning to speak proper english, and learning to conform to cultural norms in the new society does not in any way betray their self identity.

So what's the main point of all this?

It seems quite clear to me that "racist" institutions are rapidly becoming a thing of the past (in most areas at least), and the places you can still reasonably place the blame for the economic and academic disparities that exist between white America and black America are similarly rapidly dwindling.

Even when you remove poverty from the equation, the fact that black people are still doing worse in school speaks volumes about where the real contributing factors lie. The attitudes that are pervasive throughout American blacks are the real culprit, and until more people are willing to publicly stand up and admit it, there will be no significant progress toward righting the very real wealth imbalance.

Quote: DemonzLunchBreak, July 18, 2007 12:26 pm
Yeah, I guess that basically settles it.

The word I'm looking for here probably shouldn't be "free will," because that, taken literally, would mean "intent that is free from deterministic laws." That would certainly require the supernatural. I guess "free choice" is a little closer to what I'm trying to express. However, free choice makes sense as a refutation to nihilistic ideas in determinism.

I do not agree that this is settled.

I do agree with most everything that's been said so far, however, I have to quibble over the definition of free will and that robot example.

@Tsukatu, I think you're placing extra and unnecessary meaning onto the term free will by making it about the method of choice making and not the choices themselves. That's not how the term is used in general speech, and it's not really how it's used in most of the philosophical writings I've read either.

But, whatever, for the purposes of this thread, I can deal with it. If we take "free will" to mean that we have the freedom to determine how we go about forming our desires and the ability to shape our underlying programming that allows us to make choices, then sure, I don't agree that we have free will.

However, I don't think this is all that controversial of a position. And I don't think there are many people who would argue against this position either. When people present their incompatibilist arguments, this is not the position they take.

The standard incompatibilist argument is that at any given moment, whatever you are doing is the only thing that you could possibly be doing at that moment. Moreover, you actions at that moment were determined way back billions of years before you ever existed. Since your actions were determined by the past, and because the past is not up to you, then it follows that your actions are not up to you. In other words, the incompatibilist line is that you have no control over your actions if determinism is the case. Not simply that you have no control over how you make your choices.

However, here's where I take issue with everything. I don't care that my future actions can all be determined by the events of several billion years ago. It doesn't change the fact that if right at this moment, I desired to stand up, than I could stand up.

Free will, in the normal, every day use of the word, does not require that we have the ability to make choices other than we in fact made. All that it requires is the illusion that those choices were real options. As long as my actions follow my desires, then I have free will. That's what I think free will means. It doesn't mean that the will itself is free from determinism, it means that the we have the power to act according to our will.

And I believe we have that power whether or not determinism is the case.

#344856 28 2007-07-19T03:51:36Z Daddaluma
Demonz has already argued this, but the free will that you seem to be envisioning seems to me to be impossible. No matter the circumstances, free will of the sort you describe is logically impossible.

Free will, of the sort you envision, requires two contradictory things. It requires that we be able to produce outcomes that derive from our will, and yet are still unpredictable beforehand. These two things are incompatible. If an outcome is unpredictable then it means it didnt have any cause, because if it had a cause, then the outcome is necessarily predictable.

So free will of that sort is impossible. And if you insist on that being the definition for free will, then, I agree, its incompatible with determinism. Just as its incompatible with every other imaginable scenario.

This is why I say the definition of free will has to be something different.

Let me ask a quick question. Lets leave philosophy mode for a minute. When youre going about your daily life, you feel as if your actions are completely in your control right? You feel as if you have free will, dont you? Its only when you stop to think about it and argue about it here that you come to the conclusion that free will is illusory. Right?

Im fairly sure that every person feels they have free will. And that all they mean by free will is that they are free to do as they please. Or, as I said before, they have the power to act in accordance with their desires. This, is completely sufficient to describe what free will is. It is simply the power to act in accordance with your desires.

This deterministic situation where there is only one possible outcome and we in fact could not do other than we did is a total red herring. The outcome is what it is, only because we desired it to be that way. Now, its true that we dont get a say in what our desires are, but those arent usually contained in what we think of as the will.

Think about it. You cant choose to start liking mustard if you hate it. Yet no one thinks of that as an infringement on our free will. You don t get a say in the starting conditions that produce all of the desires you have, true. But that seems like the same thing as not being able to choose to like mustard. Theyre both irrelevant to what we think of as free will.

So thats my reasoning behind my defining free will as I do. Have at it.

Otherwise, you'd be running in circles with a much more plain and unarguable concept.

*shrug*

You're still hung up on that "illusion of choice" phrase I used. I take it back, let me rephrase. The choice is real, it's just that there is a choice you will make and it's the choice that you were always going to make. It doesn't mean that the other options are illusory. They were real options, it's just that you didn't take them.

Had you desired to choose otherwise, you would have.

I don't think this is even remotely an intellectually dishonest definition. I don't even see how anyone could come to apply that phrase in this situation. Intellectual dishonesty is about ignoring certain facts and reporting the truth in a biased misleading manner. I'm not doing anything of the sort.

What I'm doing is trying to argue for what I see as a much more accurate definition for free will. Free will being the term as it's used in every day conversation.

You say that free will must be the kind of thing that encompasses those two incompatible elements. I don't see why it must be. As I said, that sort of free will is logically impossible under any scenario. Ok, so if that's what free will is, then the discussion is over. Of course something that's logically impossible is going to be incompatible with determinism. It's incompatible with itself already.

What I don't see is why you feel that is must be something of that nature. Why not come up with a definition that more accurately reflects the everyday usage? If everyone basically feels free, and they call that freedom free will, then isn't it our responsibility to make a definition that fits? What do you think is so circular and unarguable about the definition I'm proposing?
